name: kappa-architecture
context: Stream-first data systems requiring unified processing for real-time and historical data with a single codebase. Best suited for organizations already using Kafka or similar streaming infrastructure.
benefits: Single codebase: One processing pipeline to maintain instead of separate batch and streaming paths
Simpler operations: No separate batch system to manage; only streaming infrastructure required
No merge complexity: Serving layer reads from single output without reconciling batch and speed layers
Easy reprocessing: Redeploy streaming job with offset=0 to recompute historical data
Consistent semantics: Same code processes both real-time events and historical replays
Reduced testing burden: One code path to test and monitor
Lower operational overhead: Single pipeline to deploy, monitor, and maintain
tradeoffs: Streaming expertise required: All processing logic must be expressed as streaming operations
Log retention cost: Full history must fit in the message queue retention policy
Reprocessing time: Replaying large historical datasets can be slower than optimized batch
Not universal: Complex batch algorithms (global sorts, full-history aggregations) may not translate to streaming
Late events handling: Watermarks and session windows add complexity
State management complexity: Stateful operators require careful RocksDB state backend design
Exactly-once complexity: Achieving exact-once semantics requires careful checkpoint coordination
use_cases: Processing logic is identical for batch and streaming workloads
Team is streaming-native with Kafka/Flink expertise
Log retention is affordable for the required data volume
Frequent reprocessing needed for logic changes or bug fixes
Building activity feeds, notifications, or analytics pipelines
avoid_when: Batch and streaming logic are fundamentally different
Historical data volume too large for queue retention
Strict exact-once guarantees require batch semantics
Reprocessing would take days while business needs hours
Global aggregations or complex algorithms that cannot be expressed incrementally
component_types: Event Log: Immutable, append-only log storing all events in order
Stream Processor: Engine reading from log and producing results
Serving Layer: Materialized views serving query results
State Backend: Persistent state storage for stateful operators
Schema Registry: Schema storage and evolution enforcement
anti_patterns: Choosing Kappa when Lambda is actually needed for complex batch workloads
Insufficient Kafka retention causing incomplete replays
Running reprocessing jobs on same cluster as live processing
Not planning atomic cutover between old and new output tables
Neglecting schema evolution for event contracts
Shared database across stream processing jobs (distributed monolith)
design_principles: Log as Source of Truth: Treat the immutable event log (Kafka/Pulsar) as the single source of truth. All historical data resides in the log; there is no separate batch store.
Unified Processing Paradigm: Express all processing logic as streaming operations. If batch and streaming logic are fundamentally different, consider Lambda instead.
Replayability First: Size log retention to cover your worst-case reprocessing window. Calculate max(replay time) × safety_factor (2x) before setting retention policies.
Semantic Preservation: Processing logic must produce identical results whether processing live events or replaying historical data. Preserve event-time semantics, watermarks, and windowing.
Atomic Cutover: When deploying new processing logic, run new and old versions in parallel until the new version catches up, then atomically switch serving layer.
Schema Evolution: Use Schema Registry with backward/forward compatibility rules. Historical events must deserialize correctly in future job versions.
Separation of Concerns: Keep reprocessing jobs on separate cluster resources from live processing to prevent resource starvation.
best_practices: Retention Sizing: Calculate worst-case reprocessing duration at 20x ingestion throughput before choosing retention. Enable tiered storage before you need it.
State Management: Use RocksDB state backend with regular checkpointing. Design state schemas for efficient fault recovery and rebalancing.
Parallelism: Scale parallelism linearly with Kafka partition count. Each partition can be processed by one task manager slot.
Schema Registry: Enforce schema compatibility (BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE or FULL) at write time. Test deserialization on sampled historical window before full replay.
Observability: Track consumer lag, processing latency, and checkpoint duration. Set up alerts for reprocessing progress.
Idempotent Writes: Design sink connectors for idempotent writes to handle exactly-once requirements and replay scenarios.
Backpressure Handling: Configure buffer sizes and timeout settings to handle varying processing speeds gracefully.
Replay Separation: Run replay jobs on separate task manager pool or during off-peak windows to avoid starving live processing.
